entries.title: A 'historically' strong El Niño is expected to make for a milder Chicago winter
entries.summary: <p>A potentially "historically strong” El Niño will make for milder winter temperatures in Chicago, according to the National Weather Service’s Winter Outlook report released Thursday.</p><p>An El Niño is a weather event that occurs when abnormally warm water temperatures in the Pacific lead to changes in weather patterns globally, specifically warmer temperatures across northern North America.</p><p>They typically occur every two to seven years. The last was in 2023 into 2024, and the current one has the potential to extend into March 2027.</p><p>“It’s probably just going to feel like any other warmer winter, especially for the latter half of the winter when the effect seems to be maximized,” said Kevin Doom, a meteorologist with the weather service. “That doesn't mean every day will be above average though, we’ll still see periods of harsh cold and wintry precipitation events.”</p><p>For the Chicago area, that means a 50 to 60% chance of above normal temperatures this winter, though the weather service said even in a mild winter to expect “notable” stretches of cold weather and snow storms.</p><p>The predicted El Niño is expected to compete with the one from the winter of 1982-83 — which raised the average winter temperature for the area by five to seven degrees and lowered snowfall by 25 to 50% — for the strongest since 1950, according to the weather service.</p><p>The report also states the weather will make for a stronger jet stream, which should largely keep polar air, the cause of polar vortexes that bring brutal stretches of chilling cold, to a minimum.</p><p>However, the report notes that “no two El Niños are alike and impacts vary.”</p><p>“It’s not a guarantee, but given this one is overly strong, confidence is pretty high [we’ll see higher temperatures],” Doom said. “This is the strongest El Niño we’ve seen in awhile, at least as long as I’ve been around.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">[9:57 AM CDT Thursday 10/16/2026]<br>With the release of the official NOAA - NWS Winter 2026-2027 Outlook today, here are some summary slides we put together.<a href="https://x.com/hashtag/ILwx?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#ILwx</a> <a href="https://x.com/hashtag/INwx?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#INwx</a> (1/3) <a href="https://t.co/zKhqKz00jy">pic.twitter.com/zKhqKz00jy</a></p>— NWS Chicago (@NWSChicago) <a href="https://x.com/NWSChicago/status/2110746919911743535?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 15, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: 3 who beat, dragged 65-year-old man off Red Line train sought by police
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are looking for three people who beat an elderly man and then dragged him off a CTA Red Line train last Friday.</p><p>The man, 65, was on the train in the 1200 block of North Clark Street, near the Clark/Division Red Line station, when the three of them beat and dragged him off the train before spray-painting his face, police said.</p><p>The suspects were described as a man in his early 20s with a shag hair style and “5718” tattooed on his left knuckles. The other attacker was listed in his early 20s wearing a dark sweater, tan pants and earrings. They were accompanied by a woman in her early 20s wearing a brown coat, black pants and brown boots, police said.</p><p>Anyone with information can contact detectives at 312-745-4447.</p>

entries.title: Ryden Carrasco scores 3 TDs as Rauner beats Schurz in winner-take-all battle for a state playoff berth
entries.summary: <p>The Illinois High School Association’s new, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2025/12/16/ihsa-expanded-football-playoffs-illinois" >expanded state playoff format</a> removed much of the drama from the regular season. More than 300 teams knew they were bound for the postseason after picking up their third win.</p><p>That wasn’t the case for teams in the Public League White. Those teams spent most of the season believing the only way into the playoffs was to win their division and then defeat a Red conference team in a Week 9 game.</p><p>That road changed last weekend when Chicago Public Schools shuffled things around and decided to have three winner-take-all playoff qualifier games pitting six of the best White conference teams against each other.</p><p>So, Rauner, which finished second in the White West, had a shot at a second consecutive season in the state playoffs if it could beat Schurz at Lane Stadium on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/10/15/high-school-football-scores-week-8" >Thursday</a>.</p><p>The Wildcats allowed Schurz junior Terrance Broughton to return the opening kickoff 70 yards for a touchdown. But Rauner took over after that in a 58-6 running-clock win.</p><p>“That [opening kickoff touchdown] was crazy,” Wildcats junior running back/linebacker Camar Russell said. “That gave us energy and pushed us. They hit us in the mouth, and it forced us to go harder and take what is ours.”</p><p>Rauner running back/linebacker Ryden Carrasco scored three touchdowns and carried the ball 10 times for 203 yards. His 86-yard TD run early in the third quarter put Rauner (7-2) up 48-6 and started the running clock. Carrasco has rushed for more than 1,300 yards this season.</p><p>“He is different,” Wildcats coach Daron Brown said. “The guy plays the entire game. He is relentless on offense. He’s relentless on defense. He is very hard to tackle, and he has good vision. I’m excited to see where he goes. He’s only a junior. These colleges need to come take a look at him.”</p><p>Junior Camar Russell added 47 rushing yards and two touchdowns. Both scores came after big second efforts.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-9a0000" entries.title: Man, 23, fatally shot in West Englewood
entries.summary: <p>A man was fatally shot in West Englewood Thursday afternoon, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The 23-year-old man was near an alley in the 6600 block of South Loomis Boulevard at 5:45 p.m. when he was shot several times, police said. He was taken to University of Chicago Medical Center where he later died.</p><p>No one is in custody, police said. </p>

entries.title: Feds investigating 'suspicious' letter sent to Chicago election office
entries.summary: <p>The FBI is investigating a suspicious envelope that was sent to the Illinois State Board of Elections Chicago office on Thursday — one of dozens of letters that were distributed to congressional offices and state election offices across the country ahead of the November election. </p><p>The Illinois State Board of Elections on Thursday evening said the Chicago office received a “suspicious envelope,” spokesman Matt Dietrich said.</p><p>“We evacuated the office and notified law enforcement immediately,” Dietrich said in an email. “The FBI now has the envelope and our office will be open as usual tomorrow.”</p><p>A similar<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/15/envelope-suspicious-substance-maria-pappas-cook-county-fbi" target="_blank" > suspicious envelope</a> containing baking powder was delivered to Cook County Treasurer Maria Pappas’ downtown office at 118 N. Clark St. Thursday morning.</p><p>Packages containing a powdery substance led to the evacuation this week of election offices in Louisiana and Oklahoma. The Ohio secretary of state said the Postal Service intercepted a package containing a white powder and said similar mailings had been sent to election officials in multiple states. </p><p>Several states, including Idaho and Florida, said their election offices either received letters or had them intercepted, according to the Associated Press.</p><p>Some of the letters contained threats and traces of fentanyl — leading some election offices to stock up on the overdose reversal medication naloxone, the AP reported.</p><p>The investigation by the FBI, U.S. Postal Inspection Service and U.S. Capitol Police was first disclosed in a message from the Senate Sergeant at Arms obtained Thursday by The Associated Press. The notice, sent to Senate offices, said that law enforcement officials were working to intercept any additional letters, but “it is possible that some letters may reach their destinations.”</p><p>The suspicious letters come just three weeks before Election Day. Early voting in Illinois began on Sept. 24.</p>

entries.title: CPS watchdog finds sexual misconduct claims against school board candidate not substantiated, sources say
entries.summary: <p>The inspector general’s office at Chicago Public Schools has closed its recently reopened investigation into allegations that school board presidential candidate Hilario Dominguez had inappropriate conduct with a minor in 2017.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://hilarioforcps.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/oig-report_Redacted.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>According to a letter sent to Dominguez Wednesday</u></a> from the CPS Office of Student Protections and Title IX, which Dominguez posted on his campaign website, the inspector general’s office “determined that there is no actionable finding of sexual misconduct.” A lawyer for the young woman who made the allegations said she received the same information on Wednesday.</p><p>The inspector general’s office made no additional findings regarding possible CPS “policy or guidelines violations relating to this incident.” That letter says the “investigation is concluded and the matter is closed” and that no further action will be taken.</p><p>The letter is not the same as the inspector general’s report, which will elaborate on why there was no actionable finding. The school board office expects to release that document by Friday.</p><p>Sources who reviewed the inspector general’s report told WBEZ that the investigation included interviews with several staff from The Resurrection Project, the nonprofit where Dominguez worked when the alleged behavior occurred, and with staff from the CPS elementary school where he once taught. The report found there was insufficient evidence that Dominguez engaged in sexually inappropriate conduct or communication with the young woman and did not substantiate the claim.</p><p>The inspector general’s office determined the same allegations were unsubstantiated earlier this year, but <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/10/09/reopened-probe-into-cps-board-president-candidates-alleged-inappropriate-contact-with-teen-could-end-soon" target="_blank" ><u>recently decided to reopen the investigation</u></a>. The young woman who made the allegations said she was not interviewed for the original investigation and came forward because she wanted to tell her story.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://hilarioforcps.com/with-office-of-inspector-general-investigation-announcing-he-is-cleared-in-full-hilario-dominguez-recenters-race-on-competing-visions/" target="_blank" ><u>In a post on Dominguez’s campaign website</u></a>, his lawyer, Rima Kapitan, said the inspector general’s report “fully cleared” Dominguez of any wrongdoing.</p><p>The Dominguez campaign also reiterated that the allegations came from Aida Flores, who was one of Dominguez’s opponents in a race for a City Council seat in 2019. Flores is currently an assistant principal in CPS and has personal ties to the young woman who made the accusations, according to multiple sources.</p><p>“Voters who weren’t aware of the decade-old smear the Aida Flores campaign spread when I ran for alderman in 2019 deserved an answer to them being brought back this year,” Dominguez <a class="Link" href="https://hilarioforcps.com/with-office-of-inspector-general-investigation-announcing-he-is-cleared-in-full-hilario-dominguez-recenters-race-on-competing-visions/" target="_blank" ><u>wrote in a statement</u></a>. “The OIG [Office of Inspector General] has given it to them.”</p><p>Dominguez said he now wants to “re-center his campaign” on education issues “that voters deeply care about.”</p><p>The young woman’s lawyer sent letters Wednesday to the inspector general, CPS Supt. Macquline King and school board members, according to copies the lawyer provided to WBEZ. In them, the lawyer expressed concerns that the reopened investigation had reached a “hasty conclusion” and said the young woman, who is now 26, is requesting “a full independent review” of how it was conducted.</p><p>The lawyer also raised questions about why the inspector general closed its initial investigation in June and did not inform the young woman until two months after Dominguez.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/10/14/chicago-public-schools-watchdog-closes-hilario-dominguez-inquiry/?utm_source=cbnewsletters.chalkbeat.org&utm_medium=newsletter&utm_campaign=no-actionable-finding-in-investigation-of-board-candidate&_bhlid=e2d256ba6a34deab1f53935ee353ae5eb35d69f6" target="_blank" ><u>The young woman told Chalkbeat and Block Club Chicago</u></a> that while she was disappointed in the investigation’s outcome, it had been empowering to share her experience.</p><p>“Young people, your voice still has power, and you may not get justice right away, but always documenting it is important,” she told the news outlets.</p><p>Flores did not respond to a request for comment.</p><p><i>This story was updated to include information about the forthcoming CPS inspector general’s report and comment from the young woman involved in the investigation and her lawyer.</i></p>

entries.title: Previewing Week 9's top high school football games
entries.summary: <h3><b>No. 21 New Trier vs. Evanston</b></h3><p><b>7:30 p.m. Friday at Ryan Field: </b>One of the area’s top rivalries is the hottest ticket the state has seen since the heyday of the Prep Bowl decades ago. It will be the third football game ever at Northwestern’s new stadium and the first prep matchup. Evanston athletic director Chris Livatino said Thursday afternoon that more than 24,000 tickets had been sold, with more than 2,000 still available. New Trier (7-1, 1-1 Central Suburban South) has a potent offense led by Purdue commit Jackie Ryder, who has 1,780 total yards and 27 touchdowns. Evanston (5-3, 0-2) is led by Illinois-bound cornerback Justin Johnson.</p><p></p><p></p><h3><b>No. 5 Hersey at No. 13 Prospect</b></h3><p><b>7 p.m. Friday: </b>The Mid-Suburban East title is on the line. Neither team has been seriously tested en route to going 8-0 overall and 4-0 in the conference, though Prospect trailed 14-0 early last week against Buffalo Grove before winning 49-14. Hersey has the consensus No. 5 senior quarterback and No. 65 player in the country in Kentucky recruit Jake Nawrot, who has thrown for 1,864 yards and 27 touchdowns. His top targets are senior Josh Riggs and junior Jaxon St. Paul. Prospect also has a Division I quarterback in Eastern Illinois commit Jackson Cacini, who has 1,854 total yards and 23 touchdowns.</p><p></p><p></p><h3><b>No. 4 Mount Carmel at No. 1 Loyola</b></h3><p><b>6:30 p.m. Friday: </b>Loyola (8-0, 2-0 Catholic Blue) is coming off its toughest test of the season, a 45-35 victory against small-school power IC Catholic, which led 35-18 at halftime. Junior Melo Maldonado ran for 124 yards and three touchdowns for the Ramblers and junior Matthew Lee passed for 231 yards. Quarterback Brady Cloherty is having the best passing season ever at Mount Carmel (6-2, 1-1), twice throwing for a program-record seven touchdowns in a game. He’s helped by having the state’s best receiving combo in senior Quentin Burrell (Michigan) and junior Marshaun Thornton.</p><p></p><p></p><h3><b>Morgan Park vs. Kenwood</b></h3><p><b>1 p.m. Saturday at Lane: </b>For the first time, the Public League is crowning a regular-season champion by matching the winners of the top two Red divisions. Red Star winner Morgan Park (7-1) has won seven in a row after an opening loss to Downers Grove North. Safety Darrell Mattison, an Ole Miss commit, is the Public League’s top senior prospect. Junior quarterback Ronald Smith Jr. and senior running back Will Smith Jr. are a pair of impact players for the Mustangs’ offense. Kenwood (6-2) is unbeaten after starting with losses to Palatine and Providence. Junior quarterback Malachi Henigan and senior receiver Lawrence Carr, the state’s top uncommitted senior, are a productive pitch-and-catch duo.</p><p></p><p></p><h3><b>Marist at No. 3 Brother Rice</b></h3><h3></h3><p><b>7 p.m. Friday:</b> The Battle of Pulaski is one of the state’s fiercest rivalries. Rice (6-2, 1-1 Catholic Blue) has the state’s best freshman in quarterback Sam Holcomb, who has taken over the starting job after splitting time earlier in the season. He has thrown for 1,010 yards and 14 touchdowns with no interceptions and is averaging more than 10 yards per carry with seven more touchdowns. Notre Dame commit Brayden Parks and five-star junior Kameron McGee are a formidable defensive line duo. Marist (5-3, 0-2) is led by the brother duo of junior quarterback Jake Fleming and sophomore receiver Conor Fleming.</p>

entries.title: Cook County sheriff's officer sues WWE, wrestler for 'unwanted' lap dance during live show
entries.summary: <p>A Cook County sheriff's officer is suing the WWE and wrestler Montez Ford for what he said was an “unwanted sexual lap dance” while he worked security at a wrestling event in Rosemont last July.</p><p>Noel Lucas, an off-duty sheriff’s officer, was working as private security for WWE Monday Night Raw event at Allstate Arena July 6 and had been told to sit in a seat outside the ring for his post, according to the lawsuit.</p><p>Shortly after, he alleges Ford “approached him without warning, straddled him, and began repeatedly thrusting and gyrating his hips toward him in a sexually suggestive manner.” Lawyers for Lucas say the nature of the entertainment event “does not excuse the conduct or eliminate the requirement of consent.”</p><p>“Mr. Lucas was there to do his job, not to be made a part of WWE’s entertainment,” said attorney Whitney Barr, who is representing Lucas. “He had been instructed to remain at his post, and while following those instructions, a WWE performer subjected him to unwanted sexualized physical contact in front of thousands of spectators and a nationwide audience.”</p><p>The WWE didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>The lawsuit says Lucas has suffered “substantial humiliation, emotional distress, and reputational harm,” including ridicule from the public and fellow members of law enforcement after videos of the incident went viral and were posted to WWE and Ford’s social media pages. He also alleges his children have been made fun of because of the incident.</p><p>Lucas is seeking an unnamed amount in compensation for emotional distress and punitive damages. He also demanded a jury trial, according to court documents. The first hearing is set for Dec. 10 at the Daley Center.</p>

entries.title: Artyom Levshunov's goal gives Blackhawks much-needed overtime win over Jets
entries.summary: <p>The Blackhawks entered this season hoping smarter decisions in three-on-three hockey — and better luck — would improve their overtime record.</p><p>So far, so good. The Hawks clipped the Jets 4-3 in their first overtime of the season Thursday, with Artyom Levshunov sealing the victory.</p><p>It was a crazy overtime, too, with both teams trading odd-man rushes. Spencer Knight made an incredible lateral save about a minute before Levshunov's winner to avoid the Hawks going home feeling like one of last season's biggest woes — a 4-9 overtime record — was bound to repeat itself.</p><p>"The one thing we’ve talked about [in overtime] is we want 'A' chances, not 'B' chances," coach Jeff Blashill said.</p><p>"[We] don’t want to overdo it for a 'B' chance and then give up an 'A' chance. But a lot of times, when you get 'A' chances, you give up 'A's the other way if you don’t score. You need big-time players to step up and make big plays."</p><p>Levshunov has fully established his signature celebration — gleefully leaping into teammates' arms — by this point, but he comically didn't find a willing partner in Kane.</p><p>"When you see a truck like that coming in, obviously I'm not going to try and catch him, right?" Kane said, grinning. "That would be a bad decision."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">WATCH (arty) PARTY 🎉 <a href="https://t.co/8pvVZHF0uw">pic.twitter.com/8pvVZHF0uw</a></p>— Chicago Blackhawks (@NHLBlackhawks) <a href="https://x.com/NHLBlackhawks/status/2110925352130216315?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 16, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3><b>Consecutive wins</b></h3><p>The 3-5-0 Hawks are now 2-0-0 since Connor Bedard returned, although they've squandered 3-1 leads in both games before eventually pulling them out — a pattern they don't want to become habit.</p><p>Bedard ripped his first goal of the season on a five-on-three power play, and Frank Nazar also scored and showed lots of jump in his first game back from suspension. </p><p>The second and third periods were filled with sloppy, ugly hockey, though. Bedard called it "choppy," which was probably a flattering word.</p><p>"There were parts of the game that we played really good and...parts of the game where we hurt ourselves," Blashill said. "There are lessons to be learned, but you would rather learn those lessons while you win."</p><h3><b>Notes</b></h3><p>With Bowen Byram out due to an upper-body injury, Blashill inserted Ethan Del Mastro into the lineup instead of Kevin Korchinski, yet again demonstrating his preference for the less acclaimed of the two prospects.</p><p>Kane earned his 895th career assist on Bedard's goal, moving ahead of Phil Housley for the most all-time by an American-born player.</p>

entries.title: Brewers advance to World Series for first time since 1982
entries.summary: <p>LOS ANGELES — Garrett Mitchell hit a go-ahead homer in the sixth inning, Milwaukee's brilliant bullpen slammed the door late and the Brewers rallied past the Los Angeles Dodgers 6-4 on Thursday in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series to earn their first World Series trip since 1982.</p><p>No. 9 hitter David Hamilton's two-out solo shot off Edwin Díaz gave the Brewers a two-run cushion in the ninth. Hamilton had just four homers in the regular season.</p><p>“We got down early tonight and we were like, it’s going to be a great story,” Brewers captain Christian Yelich said. “We’re going to come back and win this. Like, stay together, start chipping away. And that’s exactly what they did.”</p><p>Aaron Ashby pitched three scoreless innings for a save as the Brewers erased a four-run deficit to win their first NL pennant and second overall. Milwaukee was in the American League when the franchise made its only previous World Series appearance 44 years ago, a seven-game loss to the St. Louis Cardinals.</p><p>Shohei Ohtani's first home run this postseason helped put the Dodgers ahead 4-0 in the second inning before the Brewers came back to complete a four-game sweep of the two-time defending World Series champions a year after getting swept by Los Angeles in the NLCS.</p><p>“They may have a bunch of Hall of Famers, but we’ve got a bunch of gamers — and the gamers won this week,” Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy said.</p><p>The Dodgers' goal of a three-peat — not done since the New York Yankees from 1998-2000 and never by a National League team — died with their anemic offense and injuries to Ohtani and others on their aging roster.</p><p>“I'm not used to those consolation speeches,” manager Dave Roberts said. “The thing about sports that we all love is no matter how much you prepare, you want it, there’s no guarantees.”</p><p>After topping the majors with 103 wins during the regular season, Milwaukee became the first major league club to finish a postseason sweep after getting swept by that same opponent in the previous postseason.</p><p>The Brewers also are the first team to sweep a best-of-seven postseason series in which it trailed in every game.</p><p>“There was never a doubt in that dugout what was going to happen tonight. We knew we were going to win that game,” said first baseman Jake Bauers, the NLCS MVP.</p><p>With the score tied 4-all, Mitchell fell behind 0-2 before reliever Tanner Scott threw three straight balls for a full count. Mitchell’s 409-foot leadoff drive to center field — the first homer of his career on an 0-2 count — put the Brewers ahead for the first time. Mitchell also homered in their 6-2 victory Wednesday.</p><p>“It’s absolutely surreal," Mitchell said. "You talk about the battle-tested Brewers. We went down early and the belief in that dugout got stronger and stronger.”</p><p>The Brewers’ bullpen coolly turned away multiple threats when the Dodgers had the potential tying run on base.</p><p>Winning pitcher JoJo Romero struck out Max Muncy with Kyle Tucker at third to end the sixth.</p><p>With one out in the seventh and a runner on third, Ashby struck out Ohtani swinging before Mookie Betts grounded out to end the inning. Will Smith doubled to right with one out in the eighth and was safe at third when the ball got away from Sal Frelick for an error before Ashby got Tucker to fly out and Teoscar Hernández to strike out.</p><p>“Playing with that chip on our shoulder,” Ashby said. “You don’t ever know what to expect going into a series like that last year (against the Dodgers). You don’t know how bad it can be, and then it was as bad as it was. And we came out and we survived, and we came back this year, and those guys played their tails off.”</p><p>The Brewers tied it in the fifth, when the Dodgers bullpen issued four walks and Milwaukee stole two bases. Hamilton’s single chased starter Tyler Glasnow and scored Frelick, who walked and stole second, to pull Milwaukee to 4-3.</p><p>Alex Vesia came in and promptly walked Brice Turang and William Contreras to load the bases. Vesia then walked Bauers with two outs to force in Hamilton with the tying run.</p><p>Glasnow retired his first 10 batters — six on strikeouts — before the Brewers got to him in the fourth. Turang walked, Contreras hit a ground-rule double and Bauers followed with another ground-rule double that closed Milwaukee to 4-2.</p><p>Ohtani broke out of his postseason slump with a three-run homer after Andy Pages’ RBI single in the second. The four-time MVP released weeks of pent-up frustration by raising his arms and yelling and the crowd of 49,104 joined him in celebration.</p><p>But the Brewers wouldn't be denied. And when it was over, owner Mark Attanasio thought of Milwaukee's longtime owner and beloved late broadcaster.</p><p>“It’s so important for the community, the entire state of Wisconsin,” Attanasio said. “We’re standing on shoulders of Bud Selig and Bob Uecker.”</p>

entries.title: Can Blackhawks' full-strength lineup use its speed to pressure like Jeff Blashill wants?
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> have waited years to have a forward lineup like the one they dressed for their <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/15/blackhawks-first-overtime-jets-artyom-levshunov" >overtime win</a> Thursday against the Jets.</p><p>With Connor Bedard <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/13/connor-bedard-return-blackhawks-penguins-roman-kantserov" >healthy</a>, they have a first line with three dangerous scoring threats: Bedard, Patrick Kane and Roman Kantserov. They have a smart, heavy second line — featuring Anton Frondell and Tyler Bertuzzi — that can be effective offensively and defensively.</p><p>They have a checking line — Ryan Greene centering Jordan Greenway and Cole Smith — that understands its job and performs it well. And they have three useful players in Frank Nazar (now back from suspension), Oliver Moore and Ryan Donato left over to create the final line, although their chemistry remains a work in progress.</p><p>Compared to many NHL teams, that lineup is nothing special. The Hawks still lack the Oilers' star power or the Hurricanes' depth, for example. But at least it is comparable to most NHL teams now.</p><p>"The more really good players you have in there, the better chance that — when someone is not having their best game — somebody else is having a really good game," coach Jeff Blashill said Thursday. "This lineup up front is, on paper, the best lineup we've had."</p><p>Now the Hawks need to prove that on the ice. And there's one particular thing they need to prove they can do: possess the puck.</p><p>The Hawks have spent lots of time in their defensive zone — and relatively little time in the offensive zone — so far this season. They entered Thursday ranked 28th in offensive-zone time and 32nd in shot attempts per minute (the latter stat being influenced by a strange hesitance to shoot).</p><p>But a roster this competent shouldn't get swamped as much as previous iterations did. That needs to change.</p><p>Blashill stated the reason why succinctly and honestly back on Oct. 5: "If we spend a whole bunch of time defending, all the warts that we have defensively will show up."</p><p>There certainly are defensive warts. With Bowen Byram still trying to find a rhythm in Chicago — and now sidelined by an upper-body injury — the Hawks don't have a clear No. 1 defenseman to rely upon. Nor do they have an established shutdown center like Jordan Staal or even Jason Dickinson.</p><p>Instead, they have one of the league's youngest, most inexperienced defensive corps — and one of the league's youngest, most inexperienced groups of centers.</p><p>Hawks management is aware of that weakness, which is impossible not to notice. The Hawks frequently make mistakes with defensive-zone coverage and frequently commit turnovers when trying to exit the zone, and that's probably just the way things are going to be for a while.</p><p>Management is also aware of the team's strengths: speed and work ethic. Their plan to utilize those strengths to minimize that weakness is predicated on aggressive forechecking, which in theory controls the puck and the pace of play.</p><p>"We want to be a team that is on top of people," Blashill said Thursday. "We want to use our speed to pressure. We want to be a puck-pursuit team."</p><p>The Hawks primarily use a 2-1-2 forecheck, although they can retreat into a passive 1-1-3 depending on the situation. </p><p>In the 2-1-2, two forwards pressure the opposing defenseman circling back to retrieve the puck. The "F3" provides a second layer of support, and if the first two forecheckers contest the puck, he has the freedom to spring down and join them. </p><p>It's also important for the Hawks' two defensemen to provide a third layer of support — such as stepping up to meet pucks cleared up the boards — but they should do that only if the "F3" is high enough to cover for them.</p><p>None of that worked properly during the first few games. The Hawks were either too passive (accomplishing nothing), too aggressive (conceding odd-man rushes the other way) or a mixture of both (preventing players from anticipating teammates' decisions).</p><p>"If you hesitate for more than half a second in this league, it's too late," Donato said.</p><p>They've improved as October has gone on, setting a new high water mark Tuesday when Frondell and Bertuzzi's perfect forecheck set up Teuvo Teravainen's opening goal.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="fi" dir="ltr">hyvää iltaa Hawks fans 👋 <a href="https://t.co/VttD8NMsfn">pic.twitter.com/VttD8NMsfn</a></p>— Chicago Blackhawks (@NHLBlackhawks) <a href="https://x.com/NHLBlackhawks/status/2110161914701504520?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 14, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Blashill pointed out that rolling four lines with short shifts is another key component of the strategy, since pressuring is tiring, so having four increasingly stable lines to roll should help.</p><p>But there's still ample work to do. Shot attempts aren't a perfect proxy stat for possession time, but they're a decent proxy, and the Hawks have attempted fewer shots than their opponents in seven of eight games this season.</p><p>Last season, they had fewer in 54 of 82 games. In 2024-25, they had fewer in 61 of 82. In 2023-24 — Bedard's rookie season — they had fewer in 66 of 82. It's difficult to even imagine the Hawks consistently controlling possession considering how long it has been since they did so.</p><p>Can they change that pattern this season? This lineup should be capable of it. It will come down to execution.</p><h3><b>But about breakouts...</b></h3><p>Although the Hawks recognize the defensive zone might not be their strength this season, they'll need to at least orchestrate defensive-zone breakouts more cleanly to give themselves opportunities to forecheck.</p><p>For young defenseman Sam Rinzel, who has committed a few egregious turnovers this month, the strategy to reduce turnovers is to be more selective about when to take risks on breakouts.</p><p>"You can get caught in a tough spot in the 'D'-zone sometimes," Rinzel said. "If you really can't skate out of anything, it's OK to eat [the puck] and puck protect, use your body and find a play that way."</p><p>If there is enough time and space to move the puck but there aren't any forwards open, Blashill has encouraged to the Hawks to flip it aerially into the neutral zone or bank it off the glass — which they call "space plays."</p><p>"We're fast, so any time we can make a space play and get in a footrace, we kind of want to do that," Rinzel added.</p><p>"You don't want to lose the game yourself. That's something we've ran into a little bit when we've lost, like against the Islanders. You feel like you control the game, but just a few mistakes cost you it. We can't beat ourselves."</p>

entries.title: A Chicago billionaire is now a chief foe to both Mayor Johnson and CTU. Just who is Michael Sacks?
entries.summary: <p>Four years ago, billionaire businessman Michael Sacks wrote a $200,000 check to Brandon Johnson’s inaugural committee and went to see the mayor-elect two days after his runoff victory to advise him on how to set up his administration.</p><p>When <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/09/13/chicago-mayor-brandon-johnson-announcement-reelection-bid-2027" >Johnson launched his campaign </a>for a second term last month, he named one man as his primary political opponent: Michael Sacks.</p><p>How did their once promising relationship deteriorate? And who is this Chicago power player now in the eye of the political storm in the mayoral election — and in the elected school board races that will serve as Act One?</p><p>It depends on whom you ask.</p><p>“Michael has obviously been incredibly successful in business. But he also understands that success isn't just about getting your clients a return on their investment,” said former President Barack Obama in a video naming Sacks as Crain’s Man of Year in 2025.</p><p>“It's about strengthening your community, looking out for your city, creating opportunities, and leaving the world a little bit fairer and a little bit better than you found it.”</p><p>Jackson Potter, vice president of the Chicago Teachers Union, takes a far different view. He says Sacks wears the jacket for the role he played as “primary bundler” for former Mayor Rahm Emanuel.</p><p>“He supported the mayor, or stood by silently at best, while he closed the greatest number of schools in American history in 2013, almost exclusively in the Black community,” Potter says. “It's Project 2025, Chicago-style. That dismantling of public education certainly has his fingerprints all over it. The cover-up of police murders, the closing of mental health clinics. That’s his legacy.”</p><p>Sacks, 64, has long been a fixture in political circles, and is a major Democratic donor.</p><p>He helped recruit JB Pritzker to run for governor. He was Emanuel’s point-person on economic development, finance and education funding issues — and the architect of the Neighborhood Opportunity Fund that shared the wealth of downtown development with long neglected South and West Side neighborhoods. He also was the chief fundraiser for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024-democratic-national-convention/2024/08/18/democratic-national-convention-chicago-kickoff-spotlight-jb-pritzker-kamala-harris" >Democratic National Convention</a> that Chicago hosted in 2024.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b30000" name="image-b30000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ade2034/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F98%2F1d%2F46bdbfc04101b194a19fe446dd72%2Fdnc-041323-40.JPG 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/92372db/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F98%2F1d%2F46bdbfc04101b194a19fe446dd72%2Fdnc-041323-40.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Mayor-elect Brandon Johnson speaks about the news that the Democratic National Convention will be held in Chicago in 2024, during a press conference at the Shedd Aquarium in April, 2023. Michael Sacks is behind Johnson, on the left.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>But all of those roles were, for the most part, behind-the-scenes.</p><p>That changed when Sacks started putting his fortune behind<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/09/23/as-school-board-election-nears-cps-parents-incensed-by-political-group-at-school-event" > Common Ground Collective,</a> a newly formed political action committee that has targeted Johnson’s council allies, run commercials opposing provisions of the mayor’s 2026 budget proposal, and is now supporting anti-CTU school board candidates in the upcoming election Nov. 3.</p><p>A City Council majority ultimately rejected Johnson’s corporate head tax in 2025, and Johnson blamed Sacks for the defeat, a claim Sacks has denied.</p><p>The two had already clashed over the wording of a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2024/1/31/24057161/mayor-brandon-johnson-gaza-ceasefire-resolution-raucous-debate-clears-chambers" >2024 resolution</a> calling for a ceasefire in Gaza that passed the City Council after Johnson cast the tie-breaking vote.</p><p>Johnson declined an interview for this story. But he has implied publicly that he believes his ceasefire vote sparked some of the political opposition he faces today.</p><p>"I spoke out against how the Palestinians were being treated... the genocide that has taken place. It takes a great deal of courage to take these positions, and I know firsthand, because I experienced political retribution as a result of my position,” Johnson said at a press conference over the summer.</p><p>Sacks would not agree to an on-the-record interview for this story, but instead chose to provide selective responses to questions from the Sun-Times and WBEZ.</p><h3>Sacks’ beginnings </h3><p>Sacks grew up in a 1,250-square-foot, three bedroom house in Lincolnwood. His father had a small family insurance brokerage — until the Blizzard of `67 changed everything.</p><p>During the record snowstorm that buried Chicago, Lee Sacks was walking to a neighborhood drugstore to get food and medicine for his son, Michael, who had chicken pox. He had a chance meeting with a neighbor from down the street, Judd Malkin.</p><p>They forged a friendship that ultimately led Malkin to invite Lee Sacks to provide the insurance for his new company, JMB Realty.</p><p>“Judd said, ‘We’ve got this new real estate company, why don’t you fold your business into our company? We’re going to need insurance,’” Michael Sacks told the Sun-Times for his father’s obituary. “It turned out to be wildly successful.”</p><p>With his good fortune, Lee Sacks taught his children to give back and live by the Hebrew phrase “Tikkun Olam,” which means “repairing the world,” Sacks said.</p><p>“He is driven very much by the values of helping those less fortunate. To those who are given much, much is expected. Michael lives by that ethos. That’s what I love about him,” Emanuel told the Sun-Times.</p><p>Sacks graduated from Niles West High School, got an undergraduate degree from Tulane and a law degree and an MBA from Northwestern.</p><p>In 1990, he took a job with Grosvenor, a small asset management firm in Chicago with six employees and several hundred million dollars in assets.</p><p>One of the investments in Grosvenor’s portfolio was with now infamous financier and con artist Bernie Madoff. Sacks started digging into the returns and declared them too good to be true. After an in-person meeting with Madoff in New York, Sacks says he was “very uncomfortable and had the firm redeem all capital.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-2c0000" name="image-2c0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/45c86df/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2627x1474+0+763/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F32%2F48%2F4475c31d48728378a45c520d1e7a%2F85316336sc004-madoff.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/af69409/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2627x1474+0+763/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F32%2F48%2F4475c31d48728378a45c520d1e7a%2F85316336sc004-madoff.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b1fa514/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2627x1474+0+763/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F32%2F48%2F4475c31d48728378a45c520d1e7a%2F85316336sc004-madoff.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Financier Bernard Madoff arrives at Manhattan Federal court on March 12, 2009 in New York City. Madoff is scheduled to enter a guilty plea on 11 felony counts which under federal law can result in a sentence of about 150 years." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b1fa514/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2627x1474+0+763/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F32%2F48%2F4475c31d48728378a45c520d1e7a%2F85316336sc004-madoff.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ecf0621/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2627x1474+0+763/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F32%2F48%2F4475c31d48728378a45c520d1e7a%2F85316336sc004-madoff.JPG 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b1fa514/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2627x1474+0+763/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F32%2F48%2F4475c31d48728378a45c520d1e7a%2F85316336sc004-madoff.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Financier Bernard Madoff arrives at Manhattan federal court on March 12, 2009 in New York City.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Stephen Chernin/Getty Images</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“It wasn’t hard to see” the fraud, Sacks told the Sun-Times. “I was wrong for 17 years before I was very right.”</p><p>By the age of 30, Sacks had already made his first million dollars. Within four years, he was the firm’s CEO.</p><p>Under Sacks’ 32-year leadership, Grosvenor has grown from a boutique firm in a relatively new industry to a corporation managing $91 billion in assets for a global client base with offices in New York, Los Angeles, Toronto, London, Frankfurt, Tokyo, Hong Kong, and Seoul.</p><p>Sacks currently owns a home on one of the wealthiest blocks in Chicago and has residences in Highland Park, Colorado and Florida. He travels extensively for business on a Grosvenor-owned corporate jet and reimburses the company for any private travel.</p><h3><b>Causes Sacks bankrolls</b></h3><p>Sacks has used his wealth to bankroll an array of causes, including gun violence prevention, women’s reproductive health and tax credit scholarships that allow students to attend private schools. He created the Sacks Family Scholarship fund which has provided 162 CPS students with no-loan scholarships to attend Northwestern, where he sits on the university’s Board of Trustees.</p><p>Sacks is also a founding member of the Obama Foundation, and helped save the Chicago Sun-Times at a time when the Chicago Tribune was eyeing a purchase of the newspaper.</p><p>Sacks and his wife, Cari Sacks, have used their fortune to influence local politics. Since the beginning of last year, the couple has spent $9.2 million on Illinois-specific Democratic candidates or causes, according to campaign records.</p><p>Sacks did not get involved in the 2023 mayoral race. But this election cycle he has given roughly $500,000 to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/08/02/alexi-giannoulias-chicago-mayor-candidate-2027-february-election-secretary-of-state" >mayoral challenger Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias.</a></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-940000" name="image-940000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7ff9e2e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F34%2F8b%2Fdb19d413481391a1d251fe3473a1%2Ffranshow-260803-008.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6c7ead8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F34%2F8b%2Fdb19d413481391a1d251fe3473a1%2Ffranshow-260803-008.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5ff104b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F34%2F8b%2Fdb19d413481391a1d251fe3473a1%2Ffranshow-260803-008.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias announces his run for mayor at an event in Bronzeville on the South Side, Sunday, Aug. 2, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5ff104b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F34%2F8b%2Fdb19d413481391a1d251fe3473a1%2Ffranshow-260803-008.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ccdaa60/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F34%2F8b%2Fdb19d413481391a1d251fe3473a1%2Ffranshow-260803-008.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5ff104b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F34%2F8b%2Fdb19d413481391a1d251fe3473a1%2Ffranshow-260803-008.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias announces his run for Chicago mayor at an event in Bronzeville on the South Side Aug. 2. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>More controversially, Sacks has made off-and-on contributions to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the political arm of the American lobby for Israel in Washington, D.C.</p><p>After a pause that coincided with AIPAC's opposition to Obama’s Iran nuclear deal, Sacks resumed his donations to AIPAC after the Hamas attack on Oct. 7, 2023 that killed 1,200 people in Israel, held 251 people hostage and triggered the war in Gaza.</p><p>Sacks was one of the top 100 donors to the group’s affiliated political action committee in 2024. He continued his donations even as AIPAC has been heavily criticized for its defense of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Israel’s offensive that Gaza's Health Ministry says has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians through bombardment and famine in Gaza.</p><p>Sacks defended his support for the group in an op-ed this spring, after AIPAC took heat for <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/politics/2026/02/27/aipac-pro-israel-groups-chicago-area-democratic-congressional-primaries-miller-conyears-ervin-bean-fine" target="_blank" ><u>masking millions of dollars</u></a> in spending in Illinois’ primary election through newly formed political action committees with innocuous names, to which Sacks also contributed.</p><h3><b>What brought Sacks, Emanuel together</b></h3><p>The connection with Emanuel was forged through finance.</p><p>When Emanuel left the Clinton White House, he returned to Chicago and took a job with an investment bank, Wasserstein Perella & Co.</p><p>But before he could parlay his political connections into a $16 million fortune, Emanuel needed to learn the finance business. We will see how it goes,” Sacks said.</p><p>Bill Daley, who succeeded Emanuel as White House chief of staff, says that, by attacking Sacks, the political tag team of Johnson and CTU is following a familiar playbook.</p><p>“All socialists have a boogeyman who has money. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/280a30d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5030x2823+0+266/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F02%2F5e%2F2b4b37d740e8965ba23f29a3b4c4%2Fopc-260619-15.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e17e579/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5030x2823+0+266/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F02%2F5e%2F2b4b37d740e8965ba23f29a3b4c4%2Fopc-260619-15.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/280a30d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5030x2823+0+266/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F02%2F5e%2F2b4b37d740e8965ba23f29a3b4c4%2Fopc-260619-15.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Former U.S. Secretary of Commerce Bill Daley chats with supporters before the start of the Obama Presidential Center Grand Opening Ceremony on the South Side June 18.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“He has what Brandon Johnson needs to make a boogeyman. He’s wealthy. He’s a businessman. And he’s Jewish. I’m not saying that Brandon is antisemitic. But the fact that [Sacks] is Jewish is a plus. It’s the cherry on top of the cake.”</p><p>Potter, who is Jewish, scoffed at the notion that the mayor’s or union’s attacks are antisemitic.</p><p>“Who's spending the most in school board races? Who's putting so much money behind Alexi Giannoulias? Who's putting commercials when you try to tax corporations?” Potter says. “It’s Sacks. He's put himself in the middle of all this.”</p><p>State Sen. Robert Peters (D-Chicago), who is Jewish, sees Sacks as a “public figure” and scrutiny of him as legitimate. He said that the knee-jerk defense of Sacks by leaders of some Jewish organizations is part of a “watering down of antisemitism” that distracts from incidents of real antisemitic hate.</p><p>“Sacks, who historically has not been very public, has become very public, and he is clearly not prepared for the sort of scrutiny that comes from that,” Peters said. “He seems to want to be able to apply an immense amount of scrutiny to a lot of people, but does not seem to handle that scrutiny on him very well.”</p><p> Peters saw Sacks' enmity for Johnson firsthand during their one-on-one meeting last year. It was supposed to be about Peters’ campaign for Congress. Instead, Sacks spent most of the time talking about Johnson and the CTU.</p><p>“I spent most of this meeting having to basically be like, ‘Okay, well, I'm not Brandon Johnson, and I'm not with CTU, and I don't know why we're talking about this,’” Peters said, adding it seems both sides are preoccupied with one another “while the city is facing crises.” </p><h3><b>Johnson puts Sacks in crosshairs</b></h3><p>On the day he entered the race for a second term, Johnson attacked Sacks repeatedly and by name. When asked why, Johnson said “it’s very clear the role that he played in the Emanuel administration.”</p><p>“Is he a source of pain? Ask the thousands of families that lost their public schools. Is he the source of pain? Ask the thousands of families that did not have access to public mental clinics,” Johnson said.</p><p>In a statement for this story, a spokesperson for Johnson said the mayor has “been forced to respond to Michael Sacks and his super PAC, Common Ground Collective,” that has made “the progressive movement in our city a target.”</p><p>Chicago Federation of Labor President Bob Reiter said Johnson’s portrayal of Sacks as an enemy of working people doesn’t jibe with the go-between role that Sacks has played on behalf of organized labor, in general, and working people, in particular.</p><p>Reiter recalled that Sacks helped broker a settlement that ended a strike by downtown hotel workers and was “our advocate” and “someone we could go to… if we needed to get Rahm to lighten up on an issue.”</p><p>“I don’t understand these attacks, and I don’t think it helps [Johnson’s] campaign… There’s big corporations and billionaires who proudly say they’re against working people… Michael has always been a supporter. He has always given back,” Reiter said.</p><p>Johnson’s senior adviser Jason Lee told the Sun-Times that, as Emanuel’s closest adviser, Sacks “owns” all of the major decisions that Emanuel made.</p><p>“You called me the mayor’s top adviser. And if I said to you ‘Anything that people don’t like, I had nothing to do with. I did not advise. Anything that’s good, that was me.’ You’d say, ‘That’s ridiculous.’ And you’d be right,” Lee said.</p><p>“If somebody is the chief advisor, they have to accept responsibility for all the things that happened when they were in that role — whether that’s mass school closures, the cover up of the murder of Laquan McDonald, whatever the case may be.”</p><p> Lisa Schrader, who served as Emanuel’s chief of staff and now works for Sacks, branded Lee’s claim as “absurd.” Schrader said there was “no single person involved in every conversation or decision with Rahm, let alone Michael.” </p><h3>A helping hand for Kim Foxx</h3><p>In the furor that followed the court-ordered release of the Laquan McDonald shooting video, Cook County State’s Attorney Anita Alvarez was defeated. Emanuel decided not to run for a third term as mayor. Kim Foxx was elected state’s attorney.</p><p>But when Foxx found herself in trouble during a 2020 reelection campaign after pushing for criminal justice reforms, Sacks came to her aid with $1.1 million in campaign contributions. It happened over an egg breakfast.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-3e0000" difficult campaign. I knew that there was a segment of the community, and particularly the business community — his friends and colleagues — who might have wanted a more traditional approach to criminal justice,” Foxx said.</p><p>“He appreciated what I was trying to do. That he was translating to people, for me, what it was that I was trying to do to make the system more fair and equitable, and he said that he would support me.”</p><p> Foxx first got to know Sacks during her days as chief of staff to County Board President Toni Preckwinkle. At the time, Sacks was working on the Greater Chatham Initiative. She was impressed that a billionaire businessman would care enough to invest in a neighborhood that wasn’t his own. </p><p>Emanuel has a long-standing policy of refusing to comment on his successor’s performance. But he made an angry exception in defense of his friend, Michael Sacks.</p><p>“The attack says more about them than it does about Michael Sacks,” Emanuel said of the Johnson campaign. "If they were sitting pretty, they wouldn’t be talking about this. They’re not sitting pretty because of his leadership of the city, and everybody knows it, including the entire 5th floor … There’s a pattern of a revolving door. That tells you something, it reveals something. Full stop.”</p>

entries.title: Boy, 15, fatally shot in Riverdale
entries.summary: <p>A 15-year-old boy was shot to death Thursday night in Riverdale, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The boy was found lying on the ground around 10:50 p.m. in the 600 block of West 131st Street, police said in a statement.</p><p>He suffered multiple gunshot wounds and was taken to Christ Medical Center in Oak Lawn, where he was pronounced dead, police said. His name hasn't been released. Police said no one was arrested.</p>

entries.title: A letter to the late Lindsey Graham
entries.summary: <p>Dear Lindsey,</p><p>Your body had not long been in the grave when your pal Donald Trump made the anti-Russia legislation that carried your name a nullity. Wondering how you'd feel about this if you were around to see it. The whole point of your last decade of life was the belief (or was it a rationalization?) that by truckling to Trump you could do more good than you could have by opposing him.</p><p>In your final hours, you reportedly joked that "I can't die now. I still need to do the Russia sanctions, get Iran sorted out and do Israeli-Saudi normalization." That was the Graham optimism! You were getting big things done. You were making a difference. You could torque Trump toward the light.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-430000" name="module-430000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>The Russia sanctions did indeed become law after your passing. They named the legislation after you in tribute. The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 gave the president new authority to impose tariffs on countries importing Russian oil and gas. It commands sanctions, for example, against banks or brokers who transfer funds <br></p><ol id="rte-1331abe1-c913-11f1-ba26-af7e88d41090" start="1"><li> to or from the Government of the Russian Federation, including any entity owned by the Government of the Russian Federation; or </li><li>for the direct or indirect benefit of officials of the Government of the Russian Federation.</li></ol><p>It further prohibits investment by "United States persons" in the Russian Federation, and imposes tariffs on countries that import Russian energy.<br>Belated congratulations. It must have felt, for a brief shining moment, as if you were back in the Bush years. And then, less than a month after signing that bill, Trump turned around and proclaimed a deal that would make the United States a major purchaser of Russian diesel.</p><p>Trump's supposedly "massive" diesel deal with Vladimir Putin, as David Frum notes, is trifling as an economic matter. The 2.2 million barrels of diesel he proposes to buy from Russia amount to what the U.S. consumes in less than a day.</p><p>But the purchase is massive in another way. It is a massive betrayal of everything you once stood for. It empowers the nation that has been committing war crimes in Ukraine and arming Iran (a nation with whom we are currently at war) with TNT and drone components. Every dollar we spend on Russian diesel can be spent on missiles and drones aimed not only at Kyiv and Kherson, but at the American naval base in Bahrain and at U.S. Navy ships at sea. It empowers China, which is in alliance with Russia. And it undermines America's moral authority vis-a-vis international aggressors (if anything is left of it). In one fatal stroke, Trump has confirmed the suspicion that absolutely nothing the U.S. says — even in law — can be relied upon by friend or foe. Oh, and by the way, in his desperation to reduce diesel prices (which rose due to his decision to launch the Iran war), Trump could have simply imported the fuel from Canada.</p><p>But then, you had every reason to know this was possible, even likely, before you died.</p><p>You were around when Trump said that Ukraine had started the war, and when JD Vance and Trump teamed up to insult and humiliate Volodymyr Zelensky in the Oval Office in February 2025. Remember what Trump said? He said Zelensky was going to lose the war to Russia because he "didn't have the cards." It wasn't true even then. Ukraine has proved a marvel of improvisation and scrappy resilience. But even if Ukraine had been losing, a non-sociopath American president might have thought that the answer was more support, not less.</p><p>When Zelensky asked for security guarantees, noting that Putin had broken every single one of his promises and treaties, Trump responded, "He never broke to me. He never broke to me." That was the tone of the encounter. The victim of Russia's vicious aggression adjusting to the mind-bending reality that the American president was taking Putin's side. You were OK with it, though. More than OK. You said, "Somebody asked me if I was embarrassed about President Trump. I have never been more proud of the president. I was very proud of JD Vance for standing up for our country."</p><p>Russia's invasion of Ukraine was the clearest moral and strategic story of the 21st century. Open and shut. You must have rejoiced when Sweden and Finland joined NATO, no? That is how the world of conservatives like Lindsey Graham worked. We united with our allies against aggression. But then, you had to know that Trump essentially halted American arms deliveries to Ukraine after that Oval Office disgrace (though Trump was willing to sell arms to the Europeans that would go to Ukraine) and provided only intelligence support.</p><h3>Worst possible bargain</h3><p>And then there is the matter of personal comportment. Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the U.S, like all other democratic nations, made Putin a pariah. The International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant in March 2023 for the war crime of kidnapping Ukrainian children. The European Union imposed sanctions, froze Russian assets, and began to phase out Russian oil and gas imports. You were still in the Senate then.</p><p>In the spring and summer of 2025, Trump repeatedly issued ultimata to Russia about the Ukraine war. They had two weeks, he kept saying, to prove they weren't just "tapping us along." The two-week deadline in April came and went, as did the deadline in May, and another in July. Trump kept saying he was going to do something severe. Au contraire. In August, Trump announced that he was meeting with Putin in Alaska. It was the first such meeting between the leader of a democratic nation and the Russian despot since the invasion. Trump not only rolled out the literal red carpet for Putin and arranged a military flyover, he also stood at the foot of the plane and applauded as Putin approached. The perversity is glaring. What the hell was he applauding? And of course, he never applauded for Zelensky.</p><p>You knew all of that, and you knew that Trump's followers were taking to the project of inverting morality with gusto. Tucker Carlson was hosting Holocaust deniers and "revisionist" historians who said that Hitler was misunderstood and Churchill was actually the villain of World War II. That fits perfectly with making Zelensky the villain in the Ukraine war and recasting Putin as a great potential ally.</p><p>Lindsey Graham, I hope you are at peace now, but at the risk of speaking ill of the dead, I cannot refrain from saying that you came to embody the moral cowardice and self-delusion of an entire political party. You all convinced yourselves that some good could come of being a water carrier for such a fool. If you ever really cared about America's values or even its basic welfare, you made the worst possible bargain.</p><p><i>Mona Charen is policy editor of the Bulwark and host of the “Beg to Differ” podcast.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8b0000" name="module-8b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Lent couple $4,200; they took a vacation instead of repaying me
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> A year ago, a supposed friend of mine asked to borrow some money. Her husband had left the country so he could renew his visa to come back and work. They have kids. The wife's car was repossessed while he was gone, and she had no way to get to work. She borrowed $3,000 from me to get her car back. A few months later, she borrowed another $1,200. I was a fool to give it to her, but I was thinking of her kids.</p><p>Her husband did make it back, and they are both working now. I have texted her about the money she owes me, but she just ignores me. They had enough money to take the kids to Florida recently. How do I get past the sadness? I could really use the money back. Do I just try to let it go? — <i>REGRETFUL LENDER</i></p><p><b>DEAR LENDER:</b> You should have let it go the moment you handed the money over. When a friend asks for money, it's rarely a loan. You should always consider it a gift — and be pleasantly surprised if they ever pay you back. Despite her inexcusable behavior, I'm sure this friend appreciates your kindness in saving her family from a distressing situation. It was a good deed, and I'm sorry you've been repaid with silence.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I lost my brother last year to a brain aneurysm. We were very close, and I am still struggling with it. His birthday was this month, and I spent the day honoring him. However, other family members are telling me I should be "over it" by now. Am I wrong for still experiencing grief? I wasn't aware there is a time limit. — <i>PROCESSING IT IN ALASKA</i></p><p><b>DEAR PROCESSING IT:</b> Grief isn't something that people "get over" like a case of measles or flu. When a loved one dies, the pain of that loss can remain with us to a greater or lesser degree as we adjust to the ache we feel inside. This doesn't happen on anyone else's timetable. Some people find joining a grief support group helpful. Perhaps you should consider it.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> The man I thought to be the love of my life dumped me more than 10 years ago. He's currently going through a divorce. We have been communicating for the past four years while I've been in a good relationship with someone. This lost love has expressed his feelings of loss, but I can't seem to relax and express my feelings. He will soon be divorced, and I still don't think I should give him a chance to repeat the past. Are second chances worth the risk? — <i>STAYING IN FRIEND ZONE</i></p><p><b>DEAR STAYING:</b> Second chances are sometimes worth the risk, but not always. In your case, if you are still "in a good relationship with someone" other than this ex, I'm not sure why you'd even consider rocking the boat. In fact, it may be best if you have as little contact with your ex as possible. He was no good for you then, and he can only cause trouble now.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i> </p>
entries.author: Abigail Van Buren

entries.title: Lee Bey's top 5 Open House Chicago must-see sights
entries.summary: <p>Open House Chicago, the city's annual fall spectacle, returns this weekend. And as usual, it does not disappoint.</p><p>Now in its 16th year, the free two-day event, sponsored by the Chicago Architecture Center, lets folk see the interiors of more than 200 of the city's best places and spaces — a great deal of which are normally closed to the public.</p><p>Not a bad one in the bunch. See as many of them as you can. </p><p>And there are 19 sites that weren't on last year's tours. Among my newcomer favorites is the nearly 2-acre <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/04/17/restoration-pergola-north-lawndale-historic-sears-sunken-garden" target="_blank" >Sears Sunken Garden</a> in North Lawndale, which is undergoing a large-scale renovation at 3330 W. Arthington St.</p><p>The Griffin Museum of Science and Industry is also new this year, and I recommend seeing the place. Be warned: The museum is only offering free Open House visits on Sunday — and you'll need a <a class="Link" href="https://www.griffinmsi.org/tickets" target="_blank" >complimentary ticket</a> to get in.</p><p>Yes, I know. I’ve been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/09/21/griffin-museum-science-industry-design-ramsa-drawing-board" target="_blank" >taking digs</a> lately at the museum for wanting to construct that hefty Welcome Hall on the building's front lawn along 57th Street. Still, the palatial, Charles Atwood-designed 1893 Greek Revival structure — with 1933 Art Moderne interiors by Alfred P. Shaw — blends architecture and purpose into one of the most magical buildings in the city.</p><p>Open House is an architecture lovers dream. And an architecture critic's dream. My job is to poke around buildings, yet I've often taken a busman's weekend at Open House to see even more, or to check out old favorites. </p><p>If you're attending the event, here are five places I Wacker Drive</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Eric Allix Rogers</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Seventeenth Church of Christ, Scientist, Downtown</h3><p>Designed by Harry Weese, this circular modernist travertine-clad church — almost resembling an inverted musical speaker ready to blast off — has been an architectural curiosity since its 1968 construction. Go inside and you'll see why the building, 55 E. Wacker Drive, is among Weese's best work with its circular seating, dramatic ceiling and an Aeolian-Skinner organ with pipes beautiful enough to pass for sculpture.</p><p>To see a full list of the 2026 Open House sites, visit <a class="Link" href="https://openhousechicago.org/" target="_blank" >openhousechicago.org</a>.</p>

entries.title: Sexual harassment scandal shapes southwest suburban Illinois House race
entries.summary: <p>A far southwest suburban statehouse election race offers a rare instance of a competitive Chicago-area district on Illinois’ heavily gerrymandered legislative map.</p><p>But the 97th House contest has been driven largely by a subject all too common in Springfield: sexual harassment.</p><p>Republican Gabby Shanahan is out to win the seat she fell short of two years ago to disgraced ex-state Rep. Harry Benton, the Plainfield Democrat who stepped down this summer amid allegations of making lewd comments <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/07/31/harry-benton-report-legislative-inspector-general-speaker-chris-welch-sexual-harassment" target="_blank" ><u>to three women</u></a>.</p><p>State Rep. Jessica Dixon Heitman is seeking a full term after Will and Kendall County Democratic Party leaders appointed her in July to replace Benton — whose alleged misbehavior raised “red flags” during her own brief 2023 stint as a contracted media relations consultant in his office, the new lawmaker has said.</p><p>Shanahan and her campaign have accused Dixon Heitman of “staying silent” on Benton’s conduct toward a young staffer who later described a litany of disturbing interactions with the ex-lawmaker. A former legislative inspector general determined Benton’s behavior broke state law.</p><p>Dixon Heitman told the <a class="Link" href="https://fwrnews.com/2026/07/21/38732/" target="_blank" ><u>Farmers Weekly Review</u></a> of Will County that she respected the wishes of the young complainant who “was very opposed to filing any sort of report.” The lawmaker also told <a class="Link" href="https://www.theillinoize.com/articles/benton-replacement-worked-office-allegations" target="_blank" ><u>The Illinoize</u></a> she “was personally affected by Rep. Benton’s behavior.”</p><p>Illinois Republicans are trying to make the same case statewide against House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch, who is facing criticism from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/08/05/welch-benton-harassment-working-group-cassidy" target="_blank" ><u>within his own Democratic caucus</u></a> for directing $1.4 million to Benton’s 2024 reelection campaign.</p><p>And it’s a recurring theme in the Capitol, where ex-Speaker Michael Madigan ceded the gavel to Welch in 2021 after a downfall precipitated in part by Madigan’s mishandling of harassment allegations in his 13th Ward political organization.</p><p>Welch maintains that while his office was aware of alleged misconduct, he had no choice but to continue backing Benton without a formal complaint to spur an investigation. The speaker booted Benton from the caucus this February when another woman filed a complaint.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-7b0000" name="image-7b0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4fe2d91/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7535x4229+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F54%2F9e%2F1420870843b7be94084ba0047f34%2Fpritzkerbudget-260627-23.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a37a866/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7535x4229+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F54%2F9e%2F1420870843b7be94084ba0047f34%2Fpritzkerbudget-260627-23.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/94e4018/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7535x4229+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F54%2F9e%2F1420870843b7be94084ba0047f34%2Fpritzkerbudget-260627-23.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Illinois House Speaker Emanuel "Chris" Welch speaks at a June 16 news conference.
